content:
We have observed experimental 13C NMR: 168.60, 143.85, 130.30, 22.80, 21.35, 19.20.

We need to find SMILES that matches these shifts. The simulated for C/C=C/CCOC=O gave 161.19,130.30,124.90,62.28,26.89,17.90. Not matching well: we have 168.60 vs 161.19, 143.85 vs none, 130.30 matches, 22.80 vs 26.89, 21.35 vs 17.90, 19.20 vs none. So not good.

Simulated for CCOC(=C)OC=C gave 168.05,141.40,97.72,61.20,56.40,14.15. Observed: 168.60 close, 143.85 vs 141.40 close, 130.30 vs 97.72 not close, 22.80 vs 61.20 not close, etc. Not good.

We need a molecule with carbonyl carbon ~168-170 ppm (ester or acid), an sp2 carbon ~144 ppm (alkene), another sp2 ~130 ppm (alkene), and three aliphatic carbons around 22-21-19 ppm (likely methyls). So maybe a molecule with a carbonyl (C=O) and a conjugated double bond, plus three methyl groups.

C6H10O2 formula suggests maybe methyl acrylate (CH2=CH-COOCH3) which is C4H6O2? Actually methyl acrylate is C4H6O2? Wait: CH2=CH-COOCH3 = C5H6O2? Let's compute: C5 H6 O2? Actually CH2=CH-COOCH3: C5 H6 O2? Carbons: 5, hydrogens: 6? CH2 (2 H) + CH (1 H) + CO (0) + OCH3 (3 H) = 6 H. So C5H6O2, not our formula.

C6H10O2 could be methyl crotonate (CH3-CH=CH-COOCH3). That has carbonyl (168), alkene carbons ~140 and 130, and two methyls (CH3- and OCH3) giving ~20 ppm. That matches: carbonyl ~168, alkene ~144 (CH), ~130 (CH2), methyls ~21 (CH3) and ~19 (OCH3). Also there is maybe a carbon at ~22 (CH3). So candidate: "CC=CC(=O)OC" (methyl trans-2-butenoate). SMILES: "CC=CC(=O)OC". Let's simulate.
